phonemes.desc: Short [e] plus nasal [n] — the Sumerian word for 'lord' (en), though its function here is disputed; some read it as part of a theophoric compound.
Voiceless velar stop [k] plus close front vowel [i]; the element is sometimes understood as 'place' (Sumerian ki) or as a meaningless syllable in an old name.
Voiced alveolar stop [d] plus close back rounded vowel [u]; the ending has been compared to Sumerian du 'to go' and to various onomastic patterns.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EN-kee-doo' — three light syllables with even stress; the name has no surviving pitch or length mark in the cuneiform sources.

kin.label: Sumerian
kin.form: 𒂗𒆠𒆕 (Enkidu), the name of the wild companion in the earliest poems

kin.label: Akkadian (Standard Babylonian)
kin.form: Enkidû, the form used in the twelve-tablet Epic of Gilgamesh

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Traditional interpretation 'lord of the pleasant place' (en ki du) is now widely questioned; the name may be a pre-Sumerian or foreign theonym.

pronunciation.note: Enkidu is Tier 2: the canonical form preserves only the plain Latin alphabet with initial capitalization. The cuneiform source gives no reliable vowel length or distinctive phoneme that can be registered in Unicode, and no diacritic or special letter is philologically defensible for the primary restoration. The name is therefore presented in its simplest readable form.

domains.title: The Tamed Wild Man
domains.subtitle: Wilderness, Friendship, Mortality
domains.lead: Enkidu is the man who began as a beast and became a brother. Molded from clay by the goddess Aruru, he ran with gazelles, drank at the watering hole, and broke the traps of the hunters until a woman taught him to be human. His friendship with Gilgamesh is the pivot on which the Mesopotamian epic turns: it transforms a tyrant into a seeker, and it ends with the first great lament for a dead friend in world literature.

cards.name: The Wild Man
cards.desc: Born from clay and running with animals, he is the untamed self before language, bread, and law.

cards.name: Friend and Brother
cards.desc: His bond with Gilgamesh is the epic's moral center; they fight, embrace, and never leave one another.

cards.name: Guardian of the Cedar Forest
cards.desc: He fights beside Gilgamesh against Humbaba, the demon-warden of the sacred timber.

cards.name: Mortality's Witness
cards.desc: His death — chosen by the gods as punishment — sets Gilgamesh on the quest for eternal life.

symbols.name: Clay body
symbols.meaning: His origin from the goddess's hands; humanity as shaped earth

symbols.name: Animal pelts and long hair
symbols.meaning: The wild state before Shamhat's civilizing touch

symbols.name: Watering hole
symbols.meaning: The place where wild and civilized meet; the site of his first seduction and first separation from nature

symbols.name: Cedar door
symbols.meaning: The timber he and Gilgamesh bring from the Cedar Forest; victory and hubris together

symbols.name: Bull's thigh
symbols.meaning: The insult Enkidu hurls at Ishtar after killing the Bull of Heaven

symbols.name: Dust and silence
symbols.meaning: The House of Dust he sees in his death-dream, Mesopotamia's image of the underworld

mythology.lead: Enkidu's story is told in Sumerian poems and in the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh. He is not a king or a god but the necessary other: the mirror in which Gilgamesh first sees himself, and the corpse that teaches him that no human life is endless.

myths.title: Fashioned from Clay by Aruru
myths.text:
When the people of Uruk cry out against Gilgamesh's tyranny, the gods instruct the birth-goddess Aruru to create a rival. She washes her hands, pinches off clay, and casts it into the steppe — and Enkidu is born, a wild man shaggy with hair, clothed in pelts like an animal, knowing neither people nor bread nor beer. He eats grass with the gazelles, jostles the beasts at the watering hole, and frees the game from the hunters' traps until a trapper, losing his livelihood, carries the complaint to Gilgamesh in Uruk (Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I; the older Sumerian cycle already knows him as Bilgames's companion, ETCSL 1.8.1.4–1.8.1.5).

The epic's first move is to make the problem and its answer from the same substance: tyrant and remedy are both molded, one by a mother, one by a goddess.

myths.title: Shamhat at the Watering Hole
myths.text:
Gilgamesh sends the temple-woman Shamhat to the watering hole. For six days and seven nights she lies with Enkidu in the reeds; afterward the gazelles bolt from him, and the wild beasts of the steppe flee his side — he has crossed out of nature and cannot return. She feeds him bread and strong drink, clothing his nakedness, and he becomes her pupil: speech, city ways, the wearing of garments. Shepherds take him in and teach him to guard the flocks; his strength, once spent freeing game, now drives lions and wolves from the fold. Then Shamhat tells him of Gilgamesh, of the king who oppresses Uruk, and she leads him by the hand toward the city gates (Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I).

Civilization arrives as knowledge and loss together: he gains a tongue and loses the herd, traded in a single week.

myths.title: The Wrestling Match
myths.text:
At the door of a bridal chamber Gilgamesh is about to exercise his royal right — to lie with a bride before the groom — when a stranger bars the way. They grapple in the street like two bulls, and the doorposts shatter under the force of it, until Gilgamesh throws the challenger and, breathless, stands over him. Enkidu yields with a sentence that turns the epic: 'There is no mother who bore me who can match your mother' — he acknowledges the king's greater lineage, and Gilgamesh, hearing it, embraces him as a brother (Tablet II). The tyrant has met his equal at last, and the equal has found a purpose: each becomes what the other lacked.

The fight is the friendship: the epic founds its deepest bond not on agreement but on a drawn match between equals.

myths.title: The Cedar Forest and Humbaba
myths.text:
Gilgamesh proposes the expedition that will define them: to the far Cedar Forest, to fell its sacred timber and kill its warden, Humbaba, the monster Enlil set there 'to roar like a storm-flood' and keep men at bay. Enkidu knows the country and argues against the journey — 'my friend, we have reduced the forest [in old days]... how shall we answer?' — but he will not let his friend go alone. The elders of Uruk, seeing who loves whom, charge Enkidu with a single duty: protect the king. After weeks of marching the friends corner Humbaba, and the sun-god Shamash binds him with thirteen winds; disarmed, the monster pleads for his life. It is Enkidu who urges the killing blow (Tablets III–V).

The victory is the transgression: by slaying Enlil's warden they sign the warrant one of them will pay for.

myths.title: The Bull of Heaven
myths.text:
Ishtar offers herself to Gilgamesh; he answers with a catalogue of her ruined lovers and sends her off in fury. She climbs to heaven and demands the Bull of Heaven from Anu, threatening to smash the gates of the underworld and loose the dead upon the living if refused. Anu warns that the bull means seven years of famine; Ishtar answers that she has stored grain against it. The bull descends on Uruk, and at each snort the earth opens a pit that swallows a hundred young men. The friends close on it together: Enkidu seizes the beast, Gilgamesh strikes, and it falls. Then Enkidu tears off the bull's right thigh and hurls it into Ishtar's face — 'had I caught you too, I would have treated you the same' — and the gods assemble and decree that, for these two offenses, one of the pair must die (Tablet VI).

The choice of Enkidu — the lesser, the newer man — is the epic's first great injustice, and its engine.

myths.title: The Dream of the House of Dust
myths.text:
Enkidu sickens for twelve days, and his dreams run ahead of him. In the second he sees the underworld: the House of Dust, where the dead wear feathers like birds, eat dust and clay for sustenance, and sit in darkness; he is taken before Queen Ereškigal, and the Anunnaki gods pronounce his fate. Waking, he curses the trapper and Shamhat who civilized him; then Shamash speaks from heaven — Shamhat gave you bread fit for gods and a king for a brother — and Enkidu turns his curse to a blessing. He dies in Gilgamesh's arms. His friend covers the face like a bride's, rips his hair, heaps dust on his head, and roams the steppe until, on the seventh day, a maggot falls from the corpse's nose — and Gilgamesh understands (Tablets VII–VIII).

Enkidu's last service is to be the corpse that teaches: the quest for eternal life begins at a friend's dead face.

lore.syncretism: Enkidu has no direct counterpart in later pantheons because he is not a god but a literary figure. Yet his type — the wild man civilized by love and friendship — recurs across cultures: the Greek Daphnis, the Roman Silvanus, medieval wild men of the woods, and the noble savage of Enlightenment thought. In the Epic he is sometimes read as Gilgamesh's alter ego or double, the instinctive self that the king must integrate. Some scholars compare him to the biblical Adam formed from dust, though the parallels are thematic rather than genetic.
lore.culturalLegacy: Enkidu is one of the oldest fully realized characters in literature. He gives the Epic of Gilgamesh its emotional engine: not the quest for immortality, but the love between two men and the grief of separation. In modern retellings — novels, films, comics, games, and role-playing settings — he appears as the wild companion, the voice of conscience, and the sacrifice whose death launches the hero's final trial. His trajectory from beast to beloved remains a template for stories about humanization, friendship, and loss.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Enkidu asks what it costs to become human. Before Shamhat he is innocent but alone, speechless among his animals. After her he is clothed, fed, eloquent, and friend to a king — but also mortal, exiled from the watering hole, and sentenced to die for his loyalty. Civilization, the epic suggests, is bought with separation: from the wild, from the body, from the illusion that the gods will spare those we love.

His friendship with Gilgamesh is the rare bond in which each becomes more himself by becoming less alone. Gilgamesh learns humility because Enkidu stands up to him; Enkidu learns purpose because Gilgamesh calls him outward. Their love is not romantic in the surviving text, but it is absolute: the death of one unmakes the other's world. In that sense Enkidu is the first great witness to what grief does to a human heart.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Sumerian cuneiform as 𒂗𒆠𒆕 (En-ki-du). Unlike Greek or Indic scripts, cuneiform does not encode vowel quality or stress in a way that yields a single registrable Unicode restoration. The standard Assyriological transliteration is Enkidu; variant forms include Enkimdu in some god-lists. PuniCodex therefore presents the name in plain Latin capitals, avoiding invented diacritics.

lore.archaeology: The Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh is preserved on tablets from Nineveh's Library of Ashurbanipal (British Museum K.3375 and related fragments), from Hattusa, Uruk, Sippar, and Babylon. Older Sumerian poems about Bilgames and his companion come from Nippur and Ur. Representations of the hero and his animal companion appear on cylinder seals and reliefs, though no image can be securely identified as Enkidu rather than another hairy hero or demon.
